channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You are less logical when you hold a warm drink.
item.description: A 2008 study by Williams and Bargh claimed that holding a hot cup of coffee leads to more positive social judgments, but subsequent larger, independent studies have failed to replicate the effect.

item.title: You can solve problems better when you walk away.
item.description: A 2012 study by Baird et al. found that participants who performed a different, undemanding task performed better on a creative problem-solving test than those who worked on it continuously.

item.title: Asking why makes you more stubborn than asking how.
item.description: A 2013 study found that asking someone to explain 'why' they hold a position strengthens their opposition.

item.title: Taller people earn more because you assume they lead.
item.description: A 2004 study found that each additional inch of height correlates with a significant increase in annual earnings.

item.title: You trust people with easier names more than others.
item.description: A 2012 study demonstrated that names easy to pronounce are judged as more trustworthy.

item.title: You ignore information that contradicts what you already believe.
item.description: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek out and favor information that validates your pre-existing opinions.

item.title: You are judged more by your errors than your successes.
item.description: The 'negativity bias' causes the brain to process harmful information more deeply and for a longer duration than positive information.

item.title: The first thing you see changes the entire scene.
item.description: In cinema, the 'Kuleshov Effect' demonstrates that an identical shot of an actor's neutral face is interpreted as hungry, sad, or happy based on what preceded it.

item.title: You are more likely to lie after doing something good.
item.description: The moral licensing effect causes people to engage in unethical behavior after they have recently performed an act of moral virtue.

item.title: You overestimate your future happiness based on your current state.
item.description: The 'hot-cold empathy gap' explains why you shop for groceries when hungry and purchase food you later regret.

item.title: Every decision you make is shaped by the first number.
item.description: The study was published in 'Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin', not 'Psychological Science'.

item.title: You underestimate the influence of the physical environment.
item.description: A 2008 study by Williams and Bargh suggested that holding a warm drink leads to higher interpersonal warmth ratings, but this effect has failed to replicate in subsequent research.

item.title: You act as if you know what others are thinking.
item.description: A 1998 study demonstrated that people consistently believe they are more transparent to others than they actually are.

item.title: Your brain prefers a simple solution over a perfect one.
item.description: In 1956, Herbert Simon identified that people search for an option that meets a threshold rather than the mathematical maximum.

item.title: Your future self is often a stranger you undervalue.
item.description: A 2011 fMRI study found that the neural representation of the future self is more similar to that of a stranger than to the present self.

item.title: You perceive objects as closer when you want them.
item.description: Your level of desire for a physical object influences your visual perception of how close it is to you.

item.title: You judge the morality of an action by its success.
item.description: Observers systematically rate the quality of a decision based on whether it produced a positive or negative outcome.

item.title: You are more likely to lie if you wear counterfeit goods.
item.description: Studies suggest that wearing fake luxury products can induce a feeling of inauthenticity that leads to unethical behavior.

item.title: You accept risks more when they are presented as gains.
item.description: The framing of a decision as a 'save' versus a 'loss' shifts your tolerance for risk, even when the math is identical.

item.title: You misjudge the competence of people who speak rapidly.
item.description: Listeners may perceive faster speakers as more credible and knowledgeable, but this effect is moderated by argument quality and the listener's motivation to process the message.

item.title: You mistake the ease of processing for objective truth.
item.description: People rate statements as more accurate simply because the font is easier to read.

item.title: Your brain ignores facts that contradict your current context.
item.description: The Moses illusion occurs when people fail to notice factual errors in sentences because the question contains a semantically related entity.

item.title: You overestimate your own competence when you are ignorant.
item.description: A 1999 study found that low-performers consistently rate their abilities as above average.

item.title: You think others agree with you more than they do.
item.description: A 1977 study showed that people overestimate the consensus for their own choices.

item.title: You predict future happiness based on your current state.
item.description: A 2003 review article by Wilson and Gilbert defined the impact bias, summarizing evidence from earlier studies that showed people overestimate the duration and intensity of their emotional reactions.

item.title: Holding a warm drink makes you view people warmly.
item.description: A 2008 study reported that physical warmth might increase interpersonal warmth, but subsequent independent, higher-powered studies failed to replicate this effect.

item.title: You misjudge the value of gifts you give others.
item.description: A 2009 study showed givers prioritize the price of a gift, while recipients value the thought behind it.

item.title: You are more likely to lie after doing something ethical.
item.description: Moral licensing is the subconscious process where performing a good deed makes you feel entitled to act in your own self-interest later.

item.title: You ignore evidence that contradicts your rule unless it's framed socially.
item.description: The Wason selection task demonstrates that people identify the correct logical cards with significantly higher accuracy when the rule is framed as a social contract.

item.title: Your friends' success hurts more when it involves your own talent.
item.description: The self-evaluation maintenance model suggests you feel threatened when a close friend outperforms you in a domain essential to your self-identity.

item.title: You stay silent to keep the group happy.
item.description: The desire for consensus in decision-making groups often overrides the realistic appraisal of alternatives.

item.title: Your certainty is usually a better measure of ego.
item.description: When asked to provide a range that will contain the truth, people consistently provide estimates that are too narrow.

item.title: You view your own success as someone else's loss.
item.description: Belief in a zero-sum world leads people to interpret social and economic gains as fixed pots where one person's progress requires another's failure.

item.title: You feel an unconscious pressure to justify social fairness.
item.description: People consistently defend the legitimacy of the status quo to maintain psychological stability and a sense of control.

item.title: The presence of others disrupts your ability to learn.
item.description: While an audience can improve performance on familiar, well-learned tasks, their presence often impairs performance on novel or complex ones.

item.title: You are remarkably good at ignoring what you do not want to see.
item.description: Selective perception allows individuals to interpret ambiguous actions differently to align with partisan interests, a phenomenon demonstrated in the 1954 study 'They Saw a Game' by Hastorf and Cantril.

item.title: You assume people are consistent even when they are not.
item.description: The 'Correspondence Bias' leads you to attribute behavior to personality rather than the situation.

item.title: The complexity of a task makes you procrastinate less.
item.description: Parkinson's Law of Triviality states that the time spent on any item of an agenda is in inverse proportion to the amount of money involved.

item.title: Your brain prefers a world with simple, rigid categories.
item.description: Psychological essentialism leads you to believe that objects and people have an underlying, unchanging nature.

item.title: You use your own life as the ultimate metric.
item.description: The 'Curse of Knowledge' describes your tendency to over-rely on your own perspective when judging the knowledge of others.

item.title: You support systems that reinforce your own group's dominance.
item.description: Social Dominance Orientation measures your preference for hierarchical group relations over equality.

item.title: Your attention is silently pulled toward what you fear.
item.description: An attentional bias causes the mind to demonstrate an initial orientation toward threat-related stimuli before conscious awareness.

item.title: Venting your anger makes you more aggressive, not less.
item.description: A 2002 study showed that participants who hit a punching bag to vent anger were more aggressive than those who sat quietly.

item.title: Your brain expects others to help carry your burdens.
item.description: Social Baseline Theory suggests the human brain perceives the world as requiring less effort when a social partner is present.

item.title: You misremember when events in your life actually happened.
item.description: The telescoping effect causes people to shift distant events forward in time and recent events further back.

item.title: You prefer a known failure to an unknown outcome.
item.description: Humans tend to prefer smaller, guaranteed payoffs over larger, uncertain ones in the domain of gains, but often favor risk when facing potential losses.

item.title: You are more likely to lie when you feel moral.
item.description: Mazar and Zhong (2010) found that individuals who performed or recalled virtuous actions, such as buying eco-friendly products, were subsequently more likely to cheat, a phenomenon termed moral licensing.

item.title: You assign value to objects solely through ownership.
item.description: A 1991 study found individuals value their own items at approximately twice the price (a 100% increase) they are willing to pay for an identical item.

item.title: Your focus defines the limits of your reality.
item.description: The bottleneck model of attention suggests you process only a fraction of available sensory input.

item.title: Your senses shut down to save energy over time.
item.description: Sensory adaptation occurs when your receptors decrease their response to constant, unchanging stimulation.
